title: Career Roadmap · Network Technician
summary: A Network Technician helps organisations maintain reliable connectivity between computers, servers, printers, access points and other networked devices. The work may include installing network cables, configuring basic network settings, testing connectivity, troubleshooting Wi-Fi issues, replacing faulty equipment and documenting network changes.

about.label: Primary Workplaces

blocks.text: A Network Technician helps organisations maintain reliable connectivity between computers, servers, printers, access points and other networked devices. The work may include installing network cables, configuring basic network settings, testing connectivity, troubleshooting Wi-Fi issues, replacing faulty equipment and documenting network changes.
Depending on the employer, a technician may support office networks, campus networks, internet connectivity, structured cabling, telecom equipment or data-centre infrastructure.

blocks.label: Important distinction
blocks.text: A network technician typically focuses on installation, support and troubleshooting. A network engineer generally handles more complex network design, routing, switching and infrastructure changes. A network administrator may manage broader network operations, access controls and ongoing configuration.

blocks.text: This roadmap follows a typical three-year diploma structure. Adapt it to your institution's curriculum and practical laboratory facilities.
Year 1 — Computer and Networking Foundations

blocks.label: Objective
blocks.text: Build a foundation in computer systems, operating systems and network communication.
Core subjects:
Practical activities:

items.text: Install an operating system in a permitted lab environment.
Configure IP addresses on a local test network.
Use ping, ipconfig or ip addr to inspect network connectivity.
Identify Ethernet cables, connectors, routers and switches.
Prepare a basic network diagram for a small office.

blocks.label: Year 1 outcome
blocks.text: Understand computer hardware, operating systems, basic IP networking and common connectivity tools.
Year 2 — LAN, Routing and Network Troubleshooting

blocks.label: Objective
blocks.text: Develop practical skills in local-area networking and network configuration.
Core subjects:
Practical activities:

items.text: Build a small LAN using lab equipment or a network simulator.
Configure a simulated router and switch.
Set up DHCP and test DNS resolution in a lab environment.
Create separate simulated VLANs for different departments.
Troubleshoot common issues such as incorrect IP settings, failed DNS resolution and disconnected links.

blocks.label: Year 2 outcome
blocks.text: Configure and troubleshoot small networks while understanding routing, switching and core network services.
Year 3 — Enterprise Networking and Professional Support

blocks.label: Objective
blocks.text: Prepare for entry-level network support and infrastructure roles.
Core subjects:

items.text: Wireless access points and network coverage

blocks.text: Practical activities:

items.text: Design a small enterprise network with separate departments.
Configure a simulated routing and switching environment.
Create a network inventory and IP address plan.
Build a basic network-monitoring dashboard using lab data.
Document a troubleshooting procedure for common connectivity failures.
Complete a capstone project with a network diagram, configuration notes and test results.

blocks.label: Year 3 outcome
blocks.text: Demonstrate practical network configuration, systematic troubleshooting, documentation and readiness for supervised network support work.

rows.text: Provide network configuration and name resolution
Understand traffic filtering and access control

blocks.text: Specific tools depend on the employer. Students should learn networking concepts first, then practise using the platforms available in their institution or workplace.
Project 1 — Small Office LAN Design
Beginner

blocks.label: Objective
blocks.text: Design a basic network for a small office.
Build:

items.text: A diagram showing computers, a switch, a router and a printer.
A short report explaining the network layout.

blocks.label: Skills demonstrated
blocks.text: Network fundamentals, IP addressing, documentation and basic troubleshooting.
Project 2 — VLAN and Subnetting Lab
Intermediate

blocks.label: Objective
blocks.text: Separate simulated office departments and practise network configuration.
Build:

items.text: Separate simulated networks for departments such as accounts, operations and administration.
An IP address and subnet allocation table.
VLAN and routing configurations in a simulator.
Connectivity tests for permitted and restricted traffic.

blocks.label: Skills demonstrated
blocks.text: Subnetting, switching, VLAN concepts and routing fundamentals.
Project 3 — Network Fault Diagnosis Lab
Advanced

blocks.label: Objective
blocks.text: Develop a repeatable method for diagnosing connectivity failures.
Build:

items.text: A simulated network with deliberately introduced faults.
Test cases for incorrect IP addresses, gateway problems, DNS failures and disconnected links.
A record of commands and observations.
A resolution report for each simulated issue.

blocks.label: Skills demonstrated
blocks.text: Systematic troubleshooting, network commands, fault isolation and technical reporting.
Project 4 — Network Monitoring and Asset Dashboard
Capstone

blocks.label: Objective
blocks.text: Demonstrate how a support team monitors a small network.
Build:

items.text: A simulated or authorised lab network.
An inventory of devices, addresses and roles.
A monitoring plan for device availability and selected performance indicators.
A dashboard or report showing sample status data.
An incident log with root-cause notes and resolution steps.
A network diagram and maintenance checklist.

blocks.label: Skills demonstrated
blocks.text: Monitoring, documentation, troubleshooting, reporting and operational support.
Use network simulators or isolated lab equipment for practice. Do not scan, access or reconfigure networks that you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

By the end of the diploma, the student should aim to have:

items.text: A solid understanding of TCP/IP and IPv4 subnetting.
Practical experience configuring a small network in a lab or simulator.
Knowledge of routers, switches, VLANs, DHCP and DNS.
The ability to troubleshoot common connectivity problems.
Familiarity with Windows and Linux networking commands.
Basic understanding of Wi-Fi, network security and monitoring.
Two or three network projects with diagrams and test results.
Internship or IT support exposure where available.
A networking certification or structured certification preparation, if feasible.
A CV tailored to network technician, network support or IT support roles.

blocks.text: The most practical pathway is to start as a network technician trainee or IT support technician, gain experience resolving real connectivity issues, and progress toward NOC support, network administration or network engineering.

For employability, prioritise a small enterprise network project that includes an IP address plan, subnet calculations, a network diagram, simulated VLAN and routing configurations, connectivity tests and a troubleshooting report. This demonstrates that you can do more than define networking terms—you can configure, test and explain a network systematically.
